newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: UN envoy presses on as Congo truce holds.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy presses on as Congo truce holds.

text.p: A U.N. envoy trying to cement a Congo ceasefire met faction leaders in the body-strewn capital Brazzaville and then took their messages back to peace negotiators in next-door Gabon.

French military officials securing Brazzaville airport said Mohamed Sahnoun flew off to Libreville to brief Gabon's President Omar Bongo, the chief mediator, on the outcome of talks during a one-day visit to the old French colonial capital.
"I insisted very strongly that this ceasefire should be respected and not only for three days but beyond that," Sahnoun told journalists before leaving Brazzaville.
"The political leaders assured me that they would give instructions to their troops and to their military negotiators to prolong the ceasefire as long as possible."
Sahnoun called for an intervention force and urged France to keep some troops in Brazzaville until such a force could arrive.
"I think the problem is going to be when the peace force can be deployed. I'm much more afraid of the vacuum that could exist in the short term," he said.

Sahnoun separately met President Pascal Lissouba, his armed adversary Denis Sassou Nguesso, and Bernard Kolelas, the third force in town whose militia have kept out of the fighting so far and who is also acting as a mediator, the officials said.
Wednesday was day one of a 72-hour ceasefire clinched in local talks on Tuesday while wider peace talks floundered.
"It's incredibly quiet, it's amazing," said Darcy Christen of the international Red Cross (ICRC), underscoring general surprise at how effectively the ceasefire had begun.
Fierce street battles and artillery duels flared on June 5 after Lissouba tried to disarm the "Cobras", Sassou Nguesso's militia, ahead of now forsaken July 27 presidential elections.
Some 200 bodies were collected from the streets but hundreds more lie rotting in the danger zones. A Red Cross "body commission" hopes to start picking them up from Thursday.
Military leaders from the two rival sides also agreed on Wednesday to try to open a passage through the city centre front line to let aid workers help up to 1,500 wounded people.
Some residents in devastated central parts of the city, across the Congo river from far bigger Kinshasa in ex-Zaire, used Wednesday's calm to venture out for the first time in days.

"People are tired of staying at home. In some areas life has timidly resumed," said a spokesman for Lissouba, whose authority has dwindled to a downtown area of Brazzaville. The fighting has spared the rest of the oil-rich central African country.
While the success of the first day of the truce raised hopes, diplomats said it was clear the peace was precarious.
The 72-hour ceasefire accord expires on Friday night, by which time French troops sent in to evacuate foreigners will have largely left the city and the airport they control.
One idea on the table is for an African or international force to keep the peace.

In one encouraging sign, Sassou Nguesso, a former Marxist who ran the Congo from 1979 until 1992, said he was not opposed to an international force. Paris has so far been deaf to Lissouba's entreaties that its troops should stay on.
